title: Translation workshop
intro: At this level you no longer translate words; you translate sentences, registers and whole ways of seeing. This workshop reads a short history of translation into Persian, then works through ten sentences into Persian and ten into English with a commentary on every choice: word order, ezafe chains, tone, idioms that have to be rethought from scratch. It ends with seven words that refuse to be translated – and what each of them really covers.
goals: restructure English sentences into natural Persian order, including long ezafe chains and relative clauses
choose the right register in both languages, from a formal letter to a chat with friends
replace idioms with real equivalents instead of translating them word for word
explain what تعارف، دلتنگی، غیرت، حال، صفا، قسمت and خسته نباشید cover, and translate them in context
comment on a translation: say why one version is better than another

sections.title: From Kalila and Dimna to today
sections.intro: A short essay on the long history of translation into Persian. Watch the verbs of translating – ترجمه کردن، برگرداندن، فراهم آوردن – and the essay's question: should a translator be faithful to the words or to the meaning?

sections.title: What a translator actually decides
sections.md:
Every translation between English and Persian forces the same decisions, and this workshop names them so you can make them on purpose.

1. **Order.** Persian puts the verb last, the adjectives and possessors *after* the noun, and the time before the place. English sentences have to be taken apart and rebuilt, not converted word by word.
2. **Ezafe chains.** *The director of the Persian Language Centre of the University of Tehran* is one chain in Persian – [[مدیر مرکز زبان فارسی دانشگاه تهران|modir-e markaz-e zabān-e fārsi-ye dāneshgāh-e Tehrān]] – read from the head forward. English often needs to break it up with *'s* and *of*.
3. **Register.** Persian marks politeness in the verb ([[شما بفرمایید|shomā befarmāyid]] vs [[تو بگو|to begu]]) and has separate written and spoken forms. Decide who is talking to whom before you choose a single word.
4. **Idioms.** *A piece of cake* is not a cake in Persian; it is [[مثل آب خوردن|mesl-e āb khordan|like drinking water]]. Find the idiom the other language would use – or say it plainly.
5. **Culture words.** Some words carry customs with them. For these, the only honest method is to understand the whole situation and translate *that*.

The translator Nasrollah Monshi, who made the classical Persian *Kalila and Dimna* in the 12th century, did all five: he kept the stories, but filled them with Persian verses and Persian rhythms. His version is read today not as a translation but as Persian literature.

sections.title: Rebuilding the sentence: order and ezafe chains
sections.md:
The commonest mistake in English→Persian translation is keeping English order. Persian has its own: **subject – time – manner – place – object – verb**, adjectives and possessors **after** the noun, and relative clauses introduced by [[ـی … که|-i … ke]] on the noun.

Ezafe chains run the opposite way to English *'s*: the first word is the head, and each later word narrows it. Read *the University of Tehran's language centre director* backwards and you have the Persian order: [[مدیر مرکز زبان دانشگاه تهران|modir-e markaz-e zabān-e dāneshgāh-e Tehrān]]. When a chain gets longer than five or six links, a good translator breaks it: [[مدیر مرکزی که در دانشگاه تهران زبان فارسی درس می‌دهد|modir-e markaz-i ke dar dāneshgāh-e Tehrān zabān-e fārsi dars mi-dahad]].

Some English structures have no Persian twin and must be rethought: *I like it* becomes [[از آن خوشم می‌آید|az ān khosh-am mi-āyad|it pleases me]]; *I have been learning for two years* becomes [[دو سال است که یاد می‌گیرم|do sāl ast ke yād mi-giram|it is two years that I learn]].

sections.title: Register and idioms that need rethinking
sections.md:
**Register first.** Before translating *Could you send me the file?* ask: to whom? A professor gets [[ممکن است لطفاً فایل را برایم بفرستید؟|momken ast lotfan fāyl rā barā-yam befrestid?]]; a friend gets the spoken [[فایلو برام بفرست|fāylo barām befrest]]. English *you* has one form; Persian has two (to / shomā), plus the plural of respect and a written–spoken split. A translation that gets every word right and the register wrong is a bad translation.

**Idioms second.** An idiom is a picture, and the picture rarely survives the journey. Look for the idiom the other language would use in the same situation; if none exists, say it plainly. Literal versions of idioms are the surest sign of an amateur translation – in both directions.

sections.title: Seven words that will not translate
sections.md: Each of these words has a dictionary gloss, and each gloss is wrong somewhere. Learn them as situations, not as words – and when you translate them, translate the situation.

the 'tightening of the heart' for a person, a place or a time; sadder than *missing*, warmer than *melancholy*
the urge to stand up for one's own – family, friends, country; admired as loyalty and courage, criticised as possessive jealousy
how you are (حالت چطور است؟), the mood of a moment (حال و هوا), and in speech pure enjoyment (حال کردیم 'we had a great time')

sections.title: Workshop 1: ten sentences into Persian
sections.intro: Each English sentence (in the translation line) is followed by a Persian version and a commentary. Cover the Persian, try your own version, then compare – and read the note even when you got it right.

sentences.fa: دو سال است که فارسی یاد می‌گیرم.
sentences.r: do sāl ast ke fārsi yād mi-giram.
sentences.en: I've been learning Persian for two years.
sentences.note: The English present perfect continuous becomes 'it is two years that' + present. «دو سال است فارسی یاد گرفته‌ام» would suggest the learning is finished.

sentences.fa: مردی که در خانه‌ی کناری زندگی می‌کند، مترجم است.
sentences.r: mard-i ke dar khāne-ye kenāri zendegi mi-konad, motarjem ast.
sentences.en: The man who lives next door is a translator.
sentences.note: ـی + که on the noun; the main verb waits until the end. A comma before the main verb helps the reader of a long subject.

sentences.fa: به من گفتند که جلسه لغو شده است.
sentences.r: be man goftand ke jalase laghv shode ast.
sentences.en: I was told that the meeting had been cancelled.
sentences.note: Two changes: the English passive 'I was told' becomes the impersonal 'they told me', and Persian keeps the tense of the original words (شده است, not شده بود).

sentences.fa: ممکن است لطفاً فایل را تا فردا برایم بفرستید؟
sentences.r: momken ast lotfan fāyl rā tā fardā barā-yam befrestid?
sentences.en: Could you possibly send me the file by tomorrow?
sentences.note: Register: an email to a colleague or teacher – shomā form, لطفاً, ممکن است. 'By tomorrow' is تا فردا.

sentences.fa: مثل آب خوردن است.
sentences.r: mesl-e āb khordan ast.
sentences.en: It's a piece of cake.
sentences.note: Idiom for idiom. «یک تکه کیک است» would puzzle any Iranian.

sentences.fa: دلش برای خانه خیلی تنگ شده است.
sentences.r: del-ash barā-ye khāne kheyli tang shode ast.
sentences.en: She's very homesick.
sentences.note: Persian has no adjective for 'homesick'; the heart becomes the subject and the feeling becomes a whole clause.

sentences.fa: بهتر است پیش از آن‌که باران ببارد، راه بیفتیم.
sentences.r: behtar ast pish az ān-ke bārān bebārad, rāh biyoftim.
sentences.en: We'd better leave before it rains.
sentences.note: 'We'd better' = بهتر است + subjunctive. پیش از آن‌که always takes the subjunctive, even when English uses the present.

sentences.fa: هر چه بیشتر بخوانی، بیشتر می‌فهمی.
sentences.r: har che bish-tar bekhāni, bish-tar mi-fahmi.
sentences.en: The more you read, the more you understand.
sentences.note: The pattern هر چه … ‑تر …، ‑تر …. Generic 'you' is the to-form, as in English.

sentences.fa: از مهمان‌نوازی شما سپاسگزارم.
sentences.r: az mehmān-navāzi-ye shomā sepāsgozār-am.
sentences.en: Thank you for your hospitality.
sentences.note: Formal, for a letter or a speech. Face to face most people would say «دستتان درد نکند» or «خیلی زحمت کشیدید».

sentences.fa: جسارت نباشد، ولی فکر می‌کنم اشتباه می‌کنید.
sentences.r: jesārat na-bāshad, vali fekr mi-konam eshtebāh mi-konid.
sentences.en: No offence, but I think you're wrong.
sentences.note: جسارت نباشد 'may it not be impudence' is the polite cushion before disagreeing with someone older or senior.

sections.title: Workshop 2: ten sentences into English
sections.intro: Now the other direction. Each Persian sentence has a literal reading and a translation that an English speaker would actually say. The commentary explains the jump from one to the other.

sentences.fa: دستت درد نکند.
sentences.r: dast-at dard na-konad.
sentences.en: Thanks so much (for doing that).
sentences.note: Thanks for an action – a meal, a favour, a lift. 'Thanks for all your trouble' often fits better than a bare 'thank you'.

sentences.fa: قدمتان روی چشم.
sentences.r: ghadam-etān ru-ye cheshm.
sentences.en: You're most welcome here.
sentences.note: A host's welcome. Any image of eyes in English would sound strange; translate the warmth.

sentences.fa: چشمم آب نمی‌خورد که بیاید.
sentences.r: cheshm-am āb nemi-khorad ke biyāyad.
sentences.en: I doubt he'll come.
sentences.lit: my eye doesn't drink water that he will come
sentences.note: An idiom of doubt. English needs only a plain verb – or 'I wouldn't bet on him coming'.

sentences.fa: کار از کار گذشته است.
sentences.r: kār az kār gozashte ast.
sentences.en: It's too late now.
sentences.lit: the work has passed from the work
sentences.note: Also 'what's done is done' – choose by context.

sentences.fa: هر چه شما بفرمایید.
sentences.r: har che shomā befarmāyid.
sentences.en: Whatever you think best.
sentences.note: Ta'ārof: politeness, not obedience. In English 'as you wish' can sound cold; 'whatever suits you' is closer.

sentences.fa: بی‌زحمت نمک را بدهید.
sentences.r: bi-zahmat namak rā bedahid.
sentences.en: Could you pass the salt, please?
sentences.note: Persian softens with بی‌زحمت and an imperative; English softens with a question.

sentences.fa: مادربزرگم سال گذشته به رحمت خدا رفت.
sentences.r: mādarbozorg-am sāl-e gozashte be rahmat-e khodā raft.
sentences.en: My grandmother passed away last year.
sentences.note: A respectful euphemism needs a respectful euphemism – not 'died', and not a word-for-word religious phrase.

sentences.fa: این‌جا خیلی صفا دارد.
sentences.r: in-jā kheyli safā dārad.
sentences.en: It's really lovely here.
sentences.note: صفا is the feel of a place: peaceful, fresh, friendly. 'Lovely', 'such a nice atmosphere'.

sentences.fa: قسمت این بود که همدیگر را در تهران ببینیم.
sentences.r: ghesmat in bud ke hamdigar rā dar Tehrān bebinim.
sentences.en: We were meant to meet in Tehran.
sentences.lit: the lot was this, that we see each other in Tehran
sentences.note: 'Fate' is too heavy for most contexts; 'meant to', 'it was written' (jokingly) are closer.

sentences.fa: خدا بد ندهد!
sentences.r: khodā bad na-dahad!
sentences.en: Oh no – I hope it's nothing serious!
sentences.note: Said on hearing that someone is ill or has had an accident. Translate the concern, not the blessing.

sections.title: A country of translators
sections.md:
Iran reads the world in translation. Walk down Enghelab Street in Tehran, opposite the university, and the bookshops are full of Persian versions of Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Hemingway, Márquez and Kundera – often in several competing translations, each with its loyal readers. Well-known translators are public figures, and readers will tell you *whose* translation of a novel to buy before they tell you anything about the novel.

The traffic also runs the other way. The most famous translation from Persian is Edward FitzGerald's *Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám* (1859) – so free that scholars still argue whether it is a translation or a new English poem inspired by Khayyam. FitzGerald took quatrains apart, combined them and invented lines, and yet his version made Khayyam one of the best-known poets in the English-speaking world. It is the perfect case study for this lesson's question: [[لفظ یا معنا؟|lafz yā ma'nā?|the words or the meaning?]]

Iranian cinema and television add a third tradition: **dubbing** ([[دوبله|dubleh]]). For decades foreign films have been dubbed into Persian by star voice actors, and a good dubbing team rewrites jokes, idioms and insults so that they land in Persian – a daily, very public lesson in translating the situation rather than the words.

sections.title: Tips
items: Read your Persian translation aloud without looking at the English. If it sounds like a translation, rebuild it: move the verb, split a long clause, break the ezafe chain.
Watch the false friends of structure: «توسط» for every 'by', «این است که» for 'the thing is', «در حال … بودن» for every -ing. Each is possible; none should be automatic.
When you meet a culture word (تعارف، قسمت، صفا) in a text, ask three questions: who says it, to whom, and what would an English speaker say in the same moment?
Keep a two-column notebook of idioms you meet – Persian on one side, the real English equivalent (not the literal one) on the other.
For formal English → formal Persian, a reliable recipe: shomā verbs, لطفاً or خواهشمند است, a passive or impersonal where English has 'we'.
Translating Persian into English, cut the blessings and courtesies that English does not use – but keep the warmth they carry somewhere in the sentence.

items.en: He killed two birds with one stone.
The exam was a piece of cake.
Please, help yourself – don't stand on ceremony!

items.fa: دو سال ___ که فارسی یاد می‌گیرم.
items.r: do sāl ___ ke fārsi yād mi-giram.
items.en: I've been learning Persian for two years.

items.fa: می‌خواستیم همدیگر را ببینیم، اما ___ نبود.
items.r: mi-khāstim hamdigar rā bebinim, ammā ___ na-bud.
items.en: We wanted to see each other, but it wasn't meant to be.
The woman who teaches us Persian is from Shiraz.
items.fa: خانمی که به ما فارسی درس می‌دهد، اهل شیراز است.
items.r: khānom-i ke be mā fārsi dars mi-dahad, ahl-e Shirāz ast.

items.en: I've been living in Tehran for six months.
items.fa: شش ماه است که در تهران زندگی می‌کنم.
items.r: shesh māh ast ke dar Tehrān zendegi mi-konam.

items.fa: از ترجمه‌ی شما خیلی خوشم آمد.
items.r: az tarjome-ye shomā kheyli khosh-am āmad.

items.en: Speak of the devil – here's Reza!
The more you practise, the better you speak.
items.fa: هر چه بیشتر تمرین کنی، بهتر حرف می‌زنی.
items.r: har che bish-tar tamrin koni, behtar harf mi-zani.

items.en: Thank you for all your trouble (said to a host).
items.fa: خیلی زحمت کشیدید، دستتان درد نکند.
items.r: kheyli zahmat keshidid, dast-etān dard na-konad.

sections.title: Into English: choose the best version

items.q: [[چشمم آب نمی‌خورد که قبول کند.|cheshm-am āb nemi-khorad ke ghabul konad.]]
options: My eye doesn't drink water that he accepts.
I can't see him accepting water.
items.explain: An idiom of doubt: translate the meaning, not the eye or the water.

items.q: [[صفا آوردید!|safā āvardid!]] – said by a host at the door.
options: How lovely to see you – welcome!
items.explain: A warm formula of welcome; English expresses it with 'lovely to see you'.

items.q: [[خسته نباشید!|khaste na-bāshid!]] – said to a teacher at the end of a class.
options: Thank you – that was a great class.
items.explain: It acknowledges someone's work. English thanks them for it.

items.q: [[کار از کار گذشته است.|kār az kār gozashte ast.]]
items.explain: Nothing can be changed any more: 'it's too late', 'what's done is done'.

items.q: [[بی‌زحمت در را ببندید.|bi-zahmat dar rā bebandid.]]
options: Would you mind closing the door?
items.explain: بی‌زحمت softens the imperative; English softens with a question.

items.q: Which word is the best one-word English gloss for [[دلتنگی|deltangi]] in [[دلتنگی شب‌های غربت|deltangi-ye shab-hā-ye ghorbat]]?
items.explain: غربت is being far from home, so here دلتنگی is homesickness. In other contexts it is 'missing someone' or 'longing'.

items.fa: تام هر روز با مترو به دانشگاه می‌رود.
items.r: Tām har ruz bā metro be dāneshgāh mi-ravad.
items.en: Tom goes to university by metro every day.

items.fa: کتابی که خریدم ترجمه‌ی خوبی است.
items.r: ketāb-i ke kharidam tarjome-ye khub-i ast.
items.en: The book I bought is a good translation.

items.fa: شش ماه است که در تهران زندگی می‌کنم.
items.r: shesh māh ast ke dar Tehrān zendegi mi-konam.
items.en: I've been living in Tehran for six months.

items.fa: این واژه در انگلیسی معادل دقیقی ندارد.
items.r: in vāzhe dar engelisi mo'ādel-e daghigh-i na-dārad.
items.en: This word has no exact equivalent in English.
state, mood – and in speech, fun
the warm, peaceful feel of a place
Oh no – I hope it's nothing serious!
options: Oh no – I hope it's nothing serious!
That's very bad news for you.

items.fa: به من گفتند که جلسه لغو شده است.
items.r: be man goftand ke jalase laghv shode ast.
items.en: I was told that the meeting had been cancelled.
options: I told them the meeting was cancelled.
They asked me to cancel the meeting.
I was told that the meeting had been cancelled.
